articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned the missile attack on a Panama flagged tanker carrying 24 Indian seafarers in the Strait
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned the missile attack on a Panama flagged tanker carrying 24 Indian seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz.In a statement, the ministry said 21 of the 24 Indian nationals had been safely evacuated, while two crew members were injured and one remained missing. The ministry added that the Indian Embassy in Oman was closely monitoring the ongoing search and rescue operations."We condemn the attack on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT TARA GAS in the Strait of Hormuz on 16 November 2026. Of the 24 Indian nationals on board, 21 have been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, two injured Indian crew members have been admitted to hospital, while one Indian national remains missing," the ministry said."Our Embassy in Oman is closely monitoring the ongoing search and rescue operations in coordination with the Omani authorities. We appreciate the timely assistance and support extended by the Government of Oman in the rescue efforts," it added.MEA also reiterated that the continuing attacks on shipping in the region were "worrisome" and posed a serious threat to the safety of civilian seafarers."The targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through international waterways, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," the ministry said.Earlier, in a social media post on X, Sonowal said, "All 24 Indian nationals, along with the entire 25-member crew, are completely safe with no injuries."We are continuously monitoring the situation and remain in close contact with the ship management company to ensure the ongoing security and wellbeing of our seafarers," he said.Hours later, Sonowal, in a post on X, further said that in a distressing development, the Panama-flagged LPG tanker TARA GAS was subjected to a subsequent attack, forcing the entire crew to abandon the vessel."While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing," he said."We are urgently coordinating with the ship management company and regional rescue authorities to locate our missing seafarer and ensure the immediate safety, welfare and logistical support of the rescued crew members," the minister added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary Markwayne Mullin has blamed ‘superintelligence’ (SI) – a term given by US President Donald Trump as a
articles.body: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary Markwayne Mullin has blamed ‘superintelligence’ (SI) – a term given by US President Donald Trump as a substitute for AI – for the recent outages that impacted flights, email platforms and online banking in the country. He also sent a straightforward message for Americans worried about the wave of major tech disruptions: take a breath. Mullin’s comments came on the heels of widespread digital headaches on Monday (November 16), when customers reported trouble logging into major US banks, including Wells Fargo, Chase, US Bank, and Bank of America. That same day, United Airlines was hit by a broad system outage that briefly disrupted departing flights. Last week, Microsoft 365 was hit, rendering services inaccessible.How ‘Superintelligence’ may be overloading older systemsDuring an appearance on Fox News, Mullin said: “We just have a lot of technology thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems and the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now.”He also shared a theory raised by a tech expert, not Elon Musk, who told him that (SI) may have played a role in the breakdowns – an explanation the secretary said “kind of makes sense.” According to Mullin, the expert explained that older software simply isn't built to keep pace with self-coding AI.“He said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in and it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. That’s a ripple effect,” Mullin said.He added: “It causes these systems to be overrun that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.”Defending the Trump administration’s handling of the recent tech failures, Mullin pledged to send federal resources to assist companies struggling with system breakdowns. “We are very secure, and I feel very comfortable about where we’re at,” he said.Not a cyberattack, DHS secretary saysDespite the clustering of high-profile failures, Mullin pushed back against fears of a coordinated hack, calling the incidents “individually unrelated.”“I can tell you with 98% certainty we’re not seeing the cyberattack. We’re not seeing the footprints going in. We’re not seeing the footprints going out. And so, nothing points to it being connected,” the DHS secretary said.“Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast,” Mullin noted. Those glitches followed a rough week for critical infrastructure, including a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that triggered widespread flight delays and cancellations.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, Nova Scotia boatbuilders recovered 162 kg of fiberglass from a turbine blade and used it to build a boat hull, reclaiming material headed for landfill
articles.summary: Discover how Nova Scotia boat builders recycled 162 kg of fiberglass from a wind turbine blade into a functional boat hull, demonstrating innovative sustainability solutions in maritime manufacturing.
articles.body: In 2024, a team of boat builders in Nova Scotia found a new use for material that might otherwise have ended up in a landfill. In an experiment that saw 162 kgs of fibreglass salvaged from a section of a wind turbine blade being utilised to make a boat hull, the Second Wind Project saw Resolve Composites team up with Siemens Gamesa to prove that composite materials from the wind energy sector can be recycled in boat production. According to Canada’s National Observer, Siemens Gamesa gave Resolve Composites a 20-foot section of blade in October 2023. By January 2024, Bigeau and his team had broken the blade down into 162 kg of reusable fibreglass sheets, the National Observer reports and that fibreglass was going into the hull of a Bantam Bay 17 Skiff.The Second Wind Project turned a turbine blade into boat materialThis concept was born out of a discussion that Nick Bigeau, a professional boat builder and CTO of Resolve Composites, was having thoughts about recycling old fibreglass boats using the composite material for other products when he got intrigued by the question of what to do with wind turbine blades. As described in Climate Council’s report on the project, Siemens Gamesa provided the team with a 20-foot blade section containing 27 layers of fibreglass held together by recyclable resin. The recovered material was then set aside for the construction of a Bantam Bay 17 Skiff. The project was at once a demonstration and an opportunity to refine the process by which the group recycled their material. Instead of breaking down the blade into smaller bits, the boat builders sought to recycle the fibreglass into something that would become part of another composite object.ReceTT separated fibreglass without shredding the bladeThe recycling technology of Resolve Composites is called ReceTT. According to Canada’s National Observer, the method applies a solvent to fibreglass end products to separate the resin from the fibreglass, without submerging the whole item in a tank. That separation matters because fibreglass composites are made by bonding fibreglass and resin together. After the resin hardens, the extraction of these materials from each other is not an easy task. Recycling of composite material using existing technologies may include the process of shredding the composite into smaller parts, altering the shape of the recovered material and reducing the number of possibilities for its use. ReceTT was developed so that fibreglass could be recovered as intact sheets. Bigeau told the National Observer it took him three hours to roll up all the fibreglass recovered from the blade section. It allows the manufacturing companies to use the recovered material in the production of new composite products rather than dispose of it.The project explored another use of discarded turbine bladesRecycling of wind turbine blades is not easy because of their size and composite material used for manufacturing. Disposal becomes complicated by the size and nature of the products, especially when regular recycling facilities are unable to cope with them. The Second Wind Project offered one possible solution. Through recovering useful fibre glass and using it in making a boat hull, the group was able to demonstrate how materials from the wind energy industry could be applied in maritime manufacturing.The Second Wind Project also attracted the interest of the wind energy industry. In the 2024 announcement concerning the Second Wind Project, both Resolve Composites and Siemens Gamesa were able to present the project as a collaboration between the marine manufacturing and wind energy industries. By recovering 162 kg of fibreglass, the group demonstrated how an old wind turbine blade could be used to create something new. For boat builders, it was an opportunity to see how recycling of composite materials could take place and how materials from wind energy waste could be reused.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1945, serviceman Ric Wilkinson recorded a love message for his bride from India; decades later, it was found in an attic and reunited with Joy
articles.summary: A heartwarming story of Ric Wilkinson, a serviceman who recorded a loving message for his wife Joy in 1945. The long-lost recording is rediscovered decades later, bringing emotional memories to light.
articles.body: A serviceman named Ric Wilkinson sat down in India to record a message for his wife, Joy, in October 1945. Their first anniversary was on November 21, and before that, Ric wanted Joy to hear his voice. The recording, made on a fragile 78 rpm disc, carried more than a routine wartime greeting. The serviceman reportedly spoke about the places they had shared, the time they had spent together and how much he missed her. The message, however, remained unheard for decades and was eventually discovered in an attic. In 2020, following an extensive search, it was brought to Joy.A wedding before Ric’s deploymentAccording to the Royal Air Forces Association, Ric and Joy met at a tuck-hatch canteen in Salisbury. Joy reportedly worked at the tuck-hatch canteen. Their relationship developed rapidly, and the couple soon became engaged, initially planning to get married in the spring. Those plans, however, changed when Ric was informed that he had received embarkation leave and would soon be deployed overseas. The couple then decided to prepone the wedding rather than wait till the initially planned date.Joy later recalled that Ric had wanted them to get married the following Monday after he received the deployment news. But she told him that making the arrangements on such short notice would be extremely challenging and suggested Tuesday instead. After the wedding, they managed to travel to Blackpool for their honeymoon, but their time together as newlyweds was brief. After just 21 days of marriage, Ric had to leave Joy at home as he was sent overseas for his service.Letters and occasional recorded messages became crucial ways for the couple to stay in touch. Ric’s October 1945 recording was originally intended to reach Joy before their first wedding anniversary. In the recording, he noted the date as October 15 and told her that he was sending it from India. In addition to this, he spoke about their short time as newlyweds. He reportedly described those 21 days as “heaven.” The message ended with an expression of affection and reassurance, in which he told her that he missed her and hoped to reunite with her soon.How the recording was found decades laterThe recording was part of a communications programme named Voices of the Forces. This scheme allowed servicemen to send recordings to their people waiting at home. According to the RAFA, the Army, Navy, and Air Force Institutes (NAAFI) had set up recording facilities overseas. The servicemen could either read from prepared scripts or use stock phrases, with messages limited to around 180 words. Their voices were recorded directly onto small discs, which were then placed into envelopes and posted to their intended recipients.These records were approximately five inches across and weighed less than half an ounce. With repeated playback, the fragile surfaces were at risk of deteriorating. As per the Association, a disc could be played up to 200 times before its quality started degrading. While Ric’s message survived, it eventually became separated from the people it was originally meant for.After decades, during a house clearance, the disc was discovered in an attic. A member of the public handed it to Flowerdown House, the RAFA’s Wings Breaks hotel in Weston-super-Mare. It was subsequently passed on to the Association’s head office. The hints written on the disc included an old address and Ric’s name. However, Joy’s name as the intended recipient did not have proper visibility, as it was obscured by scratches and wear.Furthermore, the Association initially struggled to find a record player that was capable of playing the 78 rpm disc. Eventually, a musician provided a suitable turntable and was able to play the audio. While this made it possible for the Association to hear Ric’s message clearly, they still had the challenge of identifying his family and finding someone to receive the record.The search leads back to JoyThe BBC programme The One Show was approached by the Association, where it shared the available information and the digitised recording in hopes that viewers might recognise Ric or help identify his relatives. The appeal gained a substantial response, and the research and search established that Ric had died many years prior, but his wife Joy was still alive.After Joy’s family contacted the programme, RAFA reported that the Association travelled to Exeter with a film crew to bring the recording to her. She was delighted to hear her late husband’s voice again after so many years. She also revealed that this was not the only recording that Ric had sent her. Joy shared that the rediscovered message had not upset her, though it did turn her heart a bit, as she had been without Ric for so long. The reunion with the record took place in January 2020, nearly 75 years after he recorded the message from India.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'She is terrified': Bilkis Bano, family leave Gujarat after SC grants bail to 2 convicts
articles.summary: AHMEDABAD: Bilkis Bano and her family had left Gujarat earlier this month after being \"terrified\" and \"shocked\" by the Supreme Court's decision to grant
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: Bilkis Bano and her family had left Gujarat earlier this month after being "terrified" and "shocked" by the Supreme Court's decision to grant bail and suspend the life sentences of two convicts in her case, a relative said on Tuesday.In an order dated October 28, the Supreme Court suspended the life sentences and granted bail to Bipin Chandra Joshi and Pradeep Mordhiya, two of the convicts in the Bilkis Bano gangrape and murder case.They were among the 11 men sentenced in 2008 by a special CBI court in Mumbai for gangraping Bano and murdering seven members of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots.In January 2024, the Supreme Court had overturned the mass remission granted to the convicts, which had led to their temporary release in 2022."She (Bano) was in Gujarat until recently, but after the Supreme Court granted bail to two of the convicts on October 28, the family left the state around November 2-3. Out of fear, the family periodically changes their place of residence, but stays in Gujarat. This time around, they decided to leave Gujarat," said her uncle Razzak Mansuri, who lives in Devgarh Baria town of Gujarat's Dahod district.Mansuri said the court's decision came as a shock to the family, as nobody had informed them about it. They learnt about the order through social media, without even Bano's lawyer being aware of it, he said."These convicts frequently return to the village while out on parole, sometimes for 15 days, sometimes for up to a month. They are currently still in the Godhra and Dahod sub-jails. One convict is currently out on a one-month parole," Mansuri said.He said Bano and her family felt that if the convicts could obtain bail in this manner, they were capable of doing anything."She is terrified," he said.According to Mansuri, Bano's family used to visit their native village of Randhikpur in Dahod district on specific occasions. Before the convicts were released on remission, they had lived in the village for around two years.Meanwhile, in a statement issued to the media, Bano said she was shocked and disbelieving of the top court's order, which she said had been passed without hearing her."I make this statement even when words come slowly through fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief. I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me. I learnt of this through press reports.""I was a young girl, just 19 years old, when my world, my baby daughter, my family, my home, my trust in humanity was brutally wrenched from me. For 24 long years since that day, I have stood up to fight for justice, for myself and for women everywhere, again and again and again. For 24 years I have searched for and found reservoirs of courage I did not know I had, only because a million voices of support and solidarity came my way," she said.A Supreme Court bench comprising Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale granted bail to the two convicts, noting that they had been in jail for more than 17 years.Bano questioned how the Supreme Court could suspend the sentences of the two men without hearing her."I have walked to courtroom after courtroom, and been grateful each time I was vindicated; each time my faith in the idea of justice was restored. I have rebuilt from the rubble of my life, with the love of family and friends. I have yearned for peace. I have learned to smile."Yet today I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win. Familiar fears are resurfacing. I am scared once again. For myself, my family, and my children. And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again. How could the honourable Supreme Court simply suspend the sentence of the men who did this to me? How could they not even inform me? How could they not even make sure my voice was heard in their courtroom?" she said.Bano said she would challenge the order, adding that her children did not deserve to spend the rest of their lives haunted by these fears and scars."I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live, and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life," she said.(With inputs from PTI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ahmedabad | Silver Rate in Ahmedabad | Bank Holidays in Ahmedabad | Public Holidays in Ahmedabad | Ahmedabad AQI | Weather in Ahmedabad | Petrol Price in Ahmedabad | Diesel Price in Ahmedabad | CNG Price in Ahmedabad | LPG Price in AhmedabadStay updated with the latest Ahmedabad news. articles.summary: The US National Security Agency's (NSA) highly classified internal communications network has gone down, CNN reported, citing six people familiar with the
articles.body: The US National Security Agency's (NSA) highly classified internal communications network has gone down, CNN reported, citing six people familiar with the matter.There is currently no evidence that the outage was caused by a cyberattack, the sources told CNN. The agency is working to assess the extent of the disruption and has introduced staggered arrival times for personnel, they added.However, the outage is not expected to affect the NSA's ability to communicate urgent intelligence to US president Donald Trump, who is travelling in Asia. A current and a former US official told CNN that multiple backup networks and other redundancies were available to maintain secure communications with the president.The network, known as NSA Net, is used by agency employees to communicate classified information internally.The cause and full extent of the disruption remain unclear. The outage comes amid a series of major technology failures affecting US companies and public services.On Friday, a widespread systems failure forced the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights nationwide for several hours, resulting in thousands of delays and cancellations. The FAA traced the disruption to a single router in Arkansas.A separate outage affecting Microsoft products last week also left users in several parts of the world unable to access services including Outlook and Teams.There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by cyberattacks. However, the incidents have highlighted the potential consequences of failures in critical technology infrastructure, particularly when they affect essential services or national security operations.What does the NSA do?The NSA is the US government's principal agency for signals intelligence and cryptology. It collects and analyses foreign signals intelligence (SIGINT) to provide information to American policymakers and military forces, while also developing cybersecurity capabilities to protect US national security systems.Its work includes identifying foreign cyber threats, securing sensitive government and military networks, and supporting the armed forces through the Central Security Service, which coordinates cryptologic assistance to the military cryptologic community.The agency also works with US allies, private companies and researchers to strengthen cybersecurity and counter threats to national security networks.You use AI every day. articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has sparked outrage after linking the Democrats’ stance on transgender athletes to the recent nationwide flight stoppage,
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has sparked outrage after linking the Democrats’ stance on transgender athletes to the recent nationwide flight stoppage, drawing criticism for shifting the focus away from problems with the country’s air traffic control system.According to The Guardian, Vance made the remarks during an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday, while discussing the funding and modernisation of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). He suggested that Democrats would need to set aside their focus on transgender athletes for the two parties to work together on rebuilding aviation infrastructure.“We could absolutely do this with Democrats in the new Congress if they set aside the ridiculous obsession with men in women's sports and did what they said they would do, which was focus on affordability and focus on rebuilding our infrastructure,” Vance said.His comments drew sharp reactions on social media, with critics accusing the vice president of bringing up transgender issues during a discussion about an aviation crisis.The remarks came days after a nationwide FAA ground stop on Friday, November 13, brought air travel across the US to a halt for several hours. More than 2,000 flights were cancelled, while thousands more were delayed, leaving passengers stranded and disrupting travel plans.The disruption was reportedly linked to communication and radar problems during a transition from older copper telecommunications lines to fibre-optic cables.Critics hit back at VanceSeveral critics took to social media to question Vance's remarks.Fred Wellman, an incoming Democratic congressman from Missouri, wrote on X: “What is this idiot talking about?”Pod Save America host Jon Favreau also criticised the vice president, posting: “HE’S SO BAD AT THIS.”Journalist Jemele Hill accused Vance of repeatedly bringing up transgender issues in unrelated discussions.“Whatever consultant keeps telling him to randomly connect any issue to trans people is just stealing money,” she wrote on X, adding that Vance appeared to be the only person obsessed with the issue.Trump administration faces questions over FAA crisisVance's comments came as the Trump administration faced criticism over its handling of the aviation disruption.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also sought to blame the previous administration, arguing during a separate Fox News interview on Monday that the Biden administration had focused more on cultural issues than aviation infrastructure.Duffy cited changes in aviation terminology, including the use of “flight deck” instead of “cockpit” and “notice to air missions” instead of “notice to airmen”, arguing that the previous administration had prioritised such changes over the functioning of the aviation system.However, the Biden administration had allocated $25 billion for air traffic modernisation through its infrastructure legislation. Congress also recently approved another $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its systems.Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said the administration had spent only about a third of the recently allocated funding.“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the finger at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” he said during an appearance on CNN's State of the Union.He added that if the administration required additional funding, it should explain and justify its request.President Donald Trump also sought to downplay Friday's disruption, telling reporters on Tuesday: “It's like when you're big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It's fine.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 95-year-old British widow faces legal costs exceeding £1 million after a 10-year fence dispute over about 45 square metres of land, despite winning damages for trespass; a judge has now dismissed her appeal
articles.summary: A 95-year-old British widow is facing legal bills of more than £1 million after spending a decade fighting her neighbours over a garden fence.
articles.body: A 95-year-old British widow is facing legal bills of more than £1 million after spending a decade fighting her neighbours over a garden fence. The High Court has rejected an appeal by Margaret Kinnear against a ruling that she must pay her own legal costs in the dispute. This is despite her having successfully won a trespass claim against the couple living next door. The dispute involved a boundary line in the wealthy village of Sissinghurst, near Tunbridge Wells in Kent. At the centre of the case was a narrow strip of land measuring around 45 square metres. A judge described the area as being of "extremely limited, if any, usable or other value."A costly decade-long legal feudNeighbours Neil and Fiona Morgan put up a new fence in late 2015, replacing an existing fence along the boundary of Mrs Kinnear's property. According to court reports, the Morgans first placed fence posts on Mrs Kinnear's land without asking her. They later removed the posts and put up a second fence. This was followed by a temporary fence that extended further onto her property. Finally, they installed a permanent fence with concrete posts in January 2016. This became known as the "third fence." The legal battle began when the Morgans sued Mrs Kinnear for damages, claiming she had destroyed their second fence. Mrs Kinnear filed a counterclaim, accusing the couple of trespassing by putting up the fences. She also asked the court to declare that the true boundary ran along a line of hedges and trees.The case went to trial at Maidstone County Court in 2021. Recorder John Dagnall dismissed the Morgans' claim and ruled that they had trespassed by building the fences. He awarded Mrs Kinnear nominal damages of £2,600. However, the judge also rejected her request to have the third fence removed. Instead, he declared that the fence would mark the new boundary and awarded her £3,250 in damages instead of ordering its removal through an injunction.Judge describes result as a 'score draw'At a later hearing about legal costs in 2024, Recorder Dagnall ruled that both sides should pay their own legal bills. He effectively described the outcome as a "score draw." This left Mrs Kinnear responsible for her entire legal bill, which was reported to exceed £1 million. The Morgans had also faced substantial legal expenses. However, they represented themselves for much of the court battle, meaning their overall costs were lower. Mrs Kinnear appealed against the decision on legal costs, arguing that she had been the real winner of the case. Her lawyers said Neil Morgan's "egregious" and "disgraceful" behaviour during the proceedings should have led the court to order the Morgans to pay her legal expenses.High Court appeal dismissedThe appeal was heard in the High Court last week by Mr Justice Tappin. Mrs Kinnear's barrister presented examples of personal insults used by Mr Morgan in court documents and communications. These included attacks on opposing lawyers, their staff and judges. In one email, he reportedly called a junior solicitor a "lying hypocritical devious arse." In a letter sent to the court, he described a Deputy District Judge as "moronic and genuinely not fit to judge vegetables at a village fete."Delivering his judgment yesterday, Mr Justice Tappin agreed that Mr Morgan's language was "deplorable and unacceptable." However, he found no reason to overturn the original judge's decision. He agreed that Recorder Dagnall had been entitled to conclude that Mr Morgan's behaviour did not justify changing the order on legal costs. The High Court judge also supported the original decision to consider Mrs Kinnear's failure to win her main argument about the location of the property boundary. Although she had won her trespass claim, she had not secured the outcome she wanted on the boundary itself.Mr Justice Tappin also expressed regret about the huge amount of time and money spent on the dispute. Reporting on the judgment, The Independent quoted Mr Justice Tappin as saying that the argument over the "sliver of grass, tree and scrub... of extremely limited, if any, usable or other value" had led to an "expenditure of time, cost and energy wholly out of proportion to the financial value of the area of land in dispute." The High Court's decision means that the 95-year-old widow must pay her own legal costs, which exceed £1 million, bringing another setback in her decade-long dispute with her neighbours.You use AI every day. articles.title: Superintelligence, rare earth minerals and more: What Trump pitched at US-Asean dinner in Manila
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday pitched American leadership in artificial intelligence, energy exports, critical minerals and defence production to
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday pitched American leadership in artificial intelligence, energy exports, critical minerals and defence production to Southeast Asian leaders at a special US-Asean summit and dinner in Manila. He called for greater regional cooperation on trade, technology and security, while assuring partners that Washington stood behind them "100 per cent".Addressing the leaders after the closing ceremony of the 49th Asean Summit, Trump described the Indo-Pacific as "one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions". He said the US was committed to the sovereignty and prosperity of its partners and urged them to work together on rare earth minerals, magnets and other critical supply chains."The United States is a Pacific nation in the true sense, and we have been engaged in trade and commerce and diplomacy across Southeast Asia for hundreds of years," Trump said."I'm here today because America is deeply committed to the success, sovereignty, and prosperity of our many friends and partners, many of whom are at this table right now, but partners in this region, and we always will be—with you always," he added.Superintelligence and rare earth pushTrump highlighted US advances in artificial intelligence, saying the country was leading the world in what he called "superintelligence". He predicted that the technology would have a greater economic impact than the Industrial Revolution and bring major medical breakthroughs."The United States is also leading the world in superintelligence, SI, and we have the world's most powerful SI ecosystem," he said."We're excited to work with every country represented here today who want to build a future for technology and unleash enormous economic growth that it brings with it."He also urged Southeast Asian countries to prioritise cooperation on rare earth minerals and magnet production. Trump later said the US would have "everything we need" in rare earths within 10 months."We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before. We’re going to catch them [China] within 10 months," he said.China imposed restrictions on rare earth exports last year during a trade dispute with Washington. The two countries reached an agreement in June aimed at restoring US access to Chinese supplies. The minerals are essential for manufacturing products ranging from electric vehicles to mobile phones.Trade deals, energy and defence commitmentsTrump announced that he had signed a new trade agreement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul shortly before the dinner. He also referred to recent trade agreements with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan and South Korea.He claimed that $22.2 trillion was being invested in the US since he took office. Trump also highlighted a newly approved liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska, backed by South Korean investment, which he said would help supply affordable energy across the Pacific.On defence, Trump pointed to expanded joint special forces training with Indonesia and deeper military cooperation with the Philippines. He also said US defence manufacturers planned to build more than 22 new facilities to produce Patriot and THAAD missile defence systems and Tomahawk missiles.The US president also referred to the "Kuala Lumpur Peace Accord" between Cambodia and Thailand, which he said had helped save "thousands and thousands of lives" by securing a ceasefire and allowing displaced people to return home."From energy to technology to security and far beyond, there's no better partner on Earth than the United States of America," Trump said.He assured the leaders that they could contact him directly if a crisis arose. "You'll call me. You'll call Marco, you'll call others, and if they don't respond, call me. I'll take your call," he said.US and Asean adopt online scam principlesEarlier, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr welcomed Trump to Manila and announced that Asean and US teams had finalised a set of principles to tackle online scams.The joint initiatives included the Principles to Tackle Online Scams, a statement on 10 public-private partnership principles and a comprehensive work plan."In anticipation of your arrival, Mr President, and we knowing your desire for results and not just talk, our staff have been working together—Asean and your staffs have been working together—and we have come to, uh, be able to finalise and have adopted the Principles to Tackle Online Scams," Marcos said.He described the agreement as an "immediate result" of the special summit.Marcos also highlighted the longstanding relationship between the Philippines and the US, noting that the two countries marked 80 years of diplomatic ties this year. He said next year would mark the 50th anniversary of Asean-US Dialogue Relations."When I'm asked, 'What is the most important part of your relationship with the United States?' I cannot answer the question because there is no part of our lives in the Philippines that is not involved with the United States in some way, in some shape or form or another," he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: US senators urge FAA to halt router upgrades after nationwide flight chaos, demand probe
articles.summary: Democratic senators in the US have urged the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause the replacement of thousands of routers across the country's
articles.body: Democratic senators in the US have urged the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause the replacement of thousands of routers across the country's air traffic control network until an investigation determines what caused last week's nationwide flight disruption.In a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Tuesday, 13 Democratic lawmakers on the Senate Commerce Committee called for a halt to further installations, citing concerns over the safety and reliability of the ongoing upgrade. They also sought a detailed explanation of the technical failure and measures to prevent a recurrence.“With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” the senators said in the letter.The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, bringing flights across the US to a halt for around four hours. The disruption led to thousands of cancellations and delays, affecting passengers at airports across the country.The agency's initial investigation pointed to problems linked to an ongoing telecommunications network upgrade involving the replacement of outdated copper wires with fibre-optic cables and old routers with newer devices.What caused the FAA disruption?The FAA said the network became unstable after excessive data flooded its systems, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds.According to the agency, a new router installed by network service provider L3Harris in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered intermittent communication and radar signal problems at several air traffic control centres.The disruption affected 17 of the country's 22 regional air traffic control centres, which manage aircraft flying at high altitudes.The FAA said the system experienced around 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming the network's ageing routers, some of which have been in operation for 25 years.The agency's network provider, L3Harris, has been replacing copper lines with fibre-optic cables and installing new routers manufactured by Juniper Networks.In their letter, the senators said they understood that the project involved replacing 3,648 routers, but only around 400 had been installed so far, with 69 operational.They called on the FAA to identify the root cause of the failure before allowing the remaining installations to proceed.FBI joins investigation as Trump seeks $50 billionThe FBI on Tuesday said it was working with the Department of Transportation, the FAA and L3Harris to investigate the incident. However, the agency said it had not taken possession of any equipment related to the disruption.The incident has also renewed questions over the state of America's ageing aviation infrastructure and the pace of efforts to modernise it.The Trump administration has blamed outdated technology for the disruption and sought additional congressional funding to overhaul the air traffic control system.Duffy has said that around $50 billion is needed to modernise the network. The White House on Tuesday sent lawmakers an updated request seeking $50.1 billion for improvements to aviation infrastructure.The proposal includes $10.1 billion for upgrading the nation's air traffic control system, along with funding for airport infrastructure, new air traffic control centres and improvements to existing FAA towers.However, Congress had already approved $12.5 billion last year for modernising critical aviation infrastructure, including replacing outdated copper wires, floppy disks and ageing radar systems.Democratic lawmakers have questioned why the administration is seeking additional funding when it has yet to fully utilise the money already approved.The latest dispute comes amid longstanding concerns over the FAA's ageing technology, with efforts to modernise the country's air traffic control network stretching back several decades.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2021, an Ohio electrical contractor paid $270,000 for nine acres previously used as a golf range, pizza shop and church; after the county challenged its business use, an appeals court revived two claims
articles.summary: An Ohio electrical contractor that paid $270,000 for a nine-acre property once used as a golf driving range, pizza shop and church has been given another
articles.body: An Ohio electrical contractor that paid $270,000 for a nine-acre property once used as a golf driving range, pizza shop and church has been given another chance to challenge county rules preventing it from running its business there. An appeals court has restored two of the company's legal claims after finding that the lower court was wrong to dismiss them.The Ohio Court of Appeals for the Twelfth District issued its ruling on 16 November 2026 in a dispute between Jackson & Jackson, LLC, and Butler County officials. The company bought the property in November 2021, intending to use its existing buildings and parking area for its electrical services business. County officials later told the company that commercial activities were not allowed under the property's residential zoning rules. In its decision, the appeals court overturned part of an earlier ruling by the Butler County Court of Common Pleas. It allowed Jackson & Jackson to continue with two of its claims, including its argument that the zoning restrictions amounted to an unconstitutional taking of private property without compensation. However, a third claim challenging the restrictions remains dismissed.The judges sent the case back to the lower court for further proceedings. They did not decide whether the county had actually violated the company's constitutional rights. Instead, they ruled that the two claims should not have been dismissed at such an early stage. According to the court decision published by Justia, the case is recorded as Dickard v. Jackson & Jackson, L.L.C., case number CA2025-07-072, and citation 2026-Ohio-4530. Judge Mary Donovan wrote the opinion, with Presiding Judge Robin N. Piper and Judge Mike Powell agreeing.A nine-acre property with several previous businessesThe disputed property covers around nine acres at 5670 West Alexandria Road in Madison Township, Butler County, Ohio. According to the Twelfth District Court of Appeals, the site has a long history of commercial and community use, even though it is located in an R-1 Suburban Residence District. A golf driving range opened on the property in 2003. A pizza business began operating alongside it in 2009, and a church started using the site in 2018. The appeals court pointed out that although commercial activities were not permitted under the zoning rules, the Butler County Auditor had listed the property's use as "Commercial".On 22 November 2021, Jackson & Jackson bought the nine-acre property from its previous owner for $270,000 through a general warranty deed. The company provides commercial electrical and emergency response services. Its work includes helping state and local governments restore power lines after storms and other emergencies. Jackson & Jackson knew about the property's earlier commercial uses before completing the purchase. It planned to use the land for part of its existing business. After buying it, the company began parking its trucks and equipment in the property's parking area. It also started using the existing office space inside one of the buildings for business activities.County challenges the company's commercial operationsThe dispute began in May 2023, when the Butler County Zoning Inspector's office sent Jackson & Jackson a notice saying it had violated zoning rules. Around 9 May 2023, Zoning Inspector Dennis Dickard told the company to stop operating its business from the property. County officials argued that commercial activities, including electrical contracting work, were not allowed under the R-1 residential zoning rules. Jackson & Jackson responded by applying for a use variance. It wanted permission to park its company vehicles on the property and use the existing building as an administrative office.On 17 August 2023, the Butler County Board of Zoning Appeals rejected the application. The company did not challenge that decision through an administrative appeal at the Butler County Court of Common Pleas. It continued operating its business from the property. Later in 2023, Dickard filed a lawsuit against Jackson & Jackson. He asked the court to issue an injunction ordering the company to stop breaking the county's zoning rules. The company filed a response and a counterclaim against the county. In December 2024, it submitted an amended counterclaim naming Dickard and the Butler County Board of Commissioners as defendants. Jackson & Jackson argued that the county's restrictions were unconstitutional when applied to its property. It described the rules as unfair and unreasonable, especially considering the property's long history of commercial use and the existing buildings designed for business activities.Company argues zoning rules amount to an illegal takingJackson & Jackson's amended counterclaim included three separate claims. The first asked the court to declare that the zoning rules were unconstitutional when applied to its property. The company based this argument on the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the US Constitution, as well as the Ohio Constitution. The company argued that preventing commercial activities ignored the property's previous uses and stopped it from earning income from the land. The second claim focused on what is known as a regulatory taking. Jackson & Jackson argued that the county had interfered with its reasonable expectations when it bought the property for business purposes. It also claimed that the restrictions had taken away the land's economic value without providing compensation.The third claim sought financial compensation under Section 1983 of federal law. The company argued that the county's actions had harmed its business and that it was entitled to payment for the alleged taking of its property. Butler County asked the trial court to dismiss all three claims. County officials argued that the federal claim had been filed too late because it was subject to a two-year deadline. They also said the company first needed to file a writ of mandamus, a legal action asking the government to carry out its duties, to begin formal property acquisition proceedings. The county further argued that Jackson & Jackson had failed to challenge the rejection of its use variance application through an administrative appeal in August 2023. The trial court agreed with the county and dismissed all three counterclaims. Jackson & Jackson then appealed the decision.Appeals court finds two claims can proceedAfter examining the three claims separately, the Twelfth District Court of Appeals found that the trial judge had made several legal mistakes. On the filing deadline, the appeals court ruled that Jackson & Jackson's federal property-taking claim was covered by Ohio's four-year time limit under Section 2305.09(E), rather than the two-year period used by the lower court. The company filed its original counterclaim on 22 May 2024. This was within the four-year period, whether the deadline began when it bought the property on 22 November 2021 or when the zoning board rejected its application on 17 August 2023. The appeals judges therefore found that the claim should not have been dismissed as too late. The judges also rejected the county's argument that the company had to file a writ of mandamus before bringing its federal claim. Referring to the US Supreme Court's 2019 decision in Knick v. Township of Scott, the appeals court explained that property owners do not have to complete state compensation procedures before filing a federal claim under Section 1983.The judges also confirmed that Ohio state courts have the authority to hear these federal claims. The appeals court then considered the company's first claim, which challenged the constitutionality of the zoning rules. It ruled that Jackson & Jackson could ask for a court declaration on this issue without first filing an administrative appeal. The judges referred to earlier Ohio Supreme Court decisions in Driscoll v. Austintown Associates and Karches v. City of Cincinnati. These cases supported the company's right to bring a constitutional challenge through a declaratory judgment action. The appeals court also found that the zoning board's rejection of the company's application in August 2023 was a final decision. This meant Jackson & Jackson could proceed with its challenge to the zoning restrictions.One claim remains dismissedAlthough the appeals court restored two of the company's claims, it refused to bring back the second one. That claim asked the court to declare that the zoning restrictions amounted to an uncompensated taking of the property, but it did not separately request compensation through that claim. The judges found that simply making such a declaration would not settle the dispute. They also explained that a claim for compensation under Ohio state law for a property taking must be brought through mandamus proceedings.The appeals court therefore agreed with the lower court that this particular claim had been correctly dismissed. In its final decision, the Twelfth District Court of Appeals upheld part of the trial court's ruling, overturned another part and sent the case back to the Butler County Court of Common Pleas. Jackson & Jackson can now continue with its constitutional challenge to the zoning rules and its federal compensation claim under Section 1983. The appeals court also divided the legal costs of the appeal, ordering the company to pay 35 per cent and Butler County to pay the remaining 65 per cent.You use AI every day. articles.title: JD Vance breaks silence on US outages, tells Americans whether they should stockpile food and water or build bunkers
articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has sought to reassure Americans amid a series of technology and infrastructure disruptions, saying there is no need to
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has sought to reassure Americans amid a series of technology and infrastructure disruptions, saying there is no need to stockpile food and water or build underground bunkers, even as he urged the country to remain prepared for unexpected emergencies. Speaking to Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday, Vance said the Trump administration did not believe a major crisis was imminent but wanted to ensure the country was equipped to deal with worst-case scenarios.“A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water. My answer to that is no. We don't see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance said.He added that the administration wanted to prevent the worst possible outcomes while making sure the country was ready if a crisis occurred.Vance's comments came after Ingraham asked whether Americans should be preparing for emergencies, pointing to recent technology outages and reports that several countries, including the UK and France, were encouraging citizens to maintain emergency supplies.JD Vance on Pentagon's 90-day preparedness plansIngraham also raised reports about Pentagon preparations to ensure military installations could operate independently of the civilian power grid for up to 90 days.Vance described the preparations as an example of responsible government planning rather than evidence that a major disaster was approaching. “A lot of what is being reported on is just basic good government, making sure that our military is prepared, God forbid, if there was a crisis,” he said. “But we don't see a crisis coming down the pipe,” he added.Vance said President Donald Trump's administration was reinvesting in the US and improving its ability to respond to emergencies.“That doesn't mean crisis is around the corner, that just means you've got a government who is actually preparing for it,” he said.Why are Americans being urged to prepare for emergencies?Vance's remarks came amid growing concerns over the reliability of critical infrastructure following several disruptions in the US.Microsoft recently experienced widespread service outages affecting products including Outlook and Microsoft 365. A separate technical problem involving FAA communications led to a nationwide flight ground stop, disrupting thousands of journeys. There have also been reports of banking service disruptions, adding to public concerns about the possibility of wider technological failures.The developments have coincided with emergency preparedness campaigns in other countries. The UK's 'Be Ready' campaign advises households to maintain essential supplies that could last at least 72 hours. Japanese authorities have also encouraged people to maintain emergency stocks of food, water and sanitation supplies.Former FBI deputy director Dan Bongino had separately urged Americans last month to prepare for potential disruptions by keeping emergency radios, batteries, food and water filtration supplies. He argued that being prepared could help reduce anxiety during uncertain times.NSA's highly classified internal network down; Charles Schwab outage reportedOn Tuesday, NSA Net, the internal network used by the security agency, went down, CNN reported. Some Charles Schwab users reported receiving a white screen showing an internal server error Tuesday morning, according to Reddit and the tracking site Downdetector.com. Users said the app was working properly.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos donates nearly $199 million worth of Amazon shares to charities, retains stock worth $226 billion; inside his $629 million philanthropy drive in 2026
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has donated 771,492 shares of the e-commerce giant, valued at approximately $198.9 million, to nonprofit organisations,
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has donated 771,492 shares of the e-commerce giant, valued at approximately $198.9 million, to nonprofit organisations, according to a regulatory filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday, November 16. The latest contribution takes his Amazon stock donations in 2026 to at least 2.44 million shares, worth approximately $629.1 million.According to a report by Forbes, the latest donation is part of a series of charitable stock contributions made by the billionaire this year. Even after the transfer, the Amazon founder holds more than 878 million shares in the company, with his direct stake valued at approximately $226.4 billion based on Monday's closing stock price.The SEC Form 4 filing shows that Bezos transferred 674,088 Amazon shares on November 12 and another 97,404 shares on November 13. Both transactions were described as “contributions to non-profit organizations”.While the filing does not identify the recipients of the donations, a separate SEC filing by the Bezos Earth Fund Foundation confirms that it received the 97,404 shares transferred on November 13. The recipients of the remaining 674,088 shares have not been publicly identified in the cited filings.The combined value of the donated shares was calculated using Amazon's closing price of $257.75 on November 16. The transfers represented approximately 0.09 per cent of the Amazon shares Bezos directly held before making the donations.Following the transactions, the filing showed that Bezos held 878,551,932 Amazon shares directly. He also has 5,087,266 shares held indirectly through certain trusts and a limited liability company wholly owned by those trusts. Bezos serves as trustee and manager of these holdings but has disclaimed beneficial ownership of the shares.How much has Jeff Bezos donated in Amazon shares in 2026?The latest contribution follows two earlier rounds of Amazon stock donations this year. According to SEC filings, Bezos donated 1,253,797 shares on May 1 and May 4. Another 415,580 shares were donated on August 25 and 26.With the latest 771,492 shares added to these transfers, Bezos has donated at least 2.44 million Amazon shares in 2026. Their combined value is estimated at approximately $629.1 million, based on Amazon's closing price on November 16.Forbes estimated Bezos' net worth at $376.7 billion as of Monday evening, placing him second on its Real-Time Billionaires list, behind Elon Musk.Jeff Bezos and wife Lauren Sanchez Bezos' philanthropic contributionsBezos' charitable giving also includes several initiatives focused on climate change, nature conservation, homelessness and education. His wife, Lauren Sanchez Bezos, has also been part of the couple's philanthropic efforts.In 2020, Bezos pledged $10 billion through the Bezos Earth Fund to support efforts to combat climate change and protect nature by 2030. The fund has awarded approximately $2.4 billion in grants so far.He also established the Day One Fund in 2018 to support homeless families and create preschools in underserved communities. Its Day 1 Families Fund awarded $102.5 million to 32 organisations in 2025.According to Forbes, Bezos and Lauren Sanchez Bezos donated an estimated $600 million in 2025. Their combined lifetime charitable contributions stood at approximately $4.7 billion through the end of 2025, placing them tenth on Forbes' list of America's top 25 philanthropists.MacKenzie Scott's donations and how they compareBezos' former wife, MacKenzie Scott, has also made significant contributions to charitable causes since their divorce in 2019. According to Forbes, Scott donated $26.4 billion to more than 2,500 organisations between their divorce and the end of 2025, placing her third on the publication's list of America's top 25 philanthropists.She gave away $7.2 billion in 2025 alone, more than any other philanthropist worldwide. Forbes described it as the largest annual amount since it began tracking major donors in 2012. By the end of 2025, Scott had given away approximately 46 per cent of her estimated net worth.Her contributions have continued in 2026. The American Indian College Fund announced a $70 million gift from Scott in October to support Native American students and tribal colleges. She has also donated $70 million to Meals on Wheels America, $42 million to Elizabeth City State University and $20 million to youth mental health nonprofit Active Minds this year.You use AI every day. articles.title: Dua Lipa bought a £6.75 million Victorian house in London in 2020, but six years later it was still being rebuilt; a basement pool, cinema and studio are part of the project now expected to finish in 2027
articles.summary: A dream home can take years to build, but for Dua Lipa, turning a prized Victorian property in north London into her ideal living space has become a
articles.body: A dream home can take years to build, but for Dua Lipa, turning a prized Victorian property in north London into her ideal living space has become a particularly lengthy affair. Six years after purchasing the £6.75 million house, the global pop star is still waiting to move in, with an ambitious renovation project involving an underground swimming pool, private cinema and music studio now expected to be completed in July 2027.The extensive redevelopment of the West Hampstead property has been years in the making, with planning disputes, conservation concerns and the technical challenges of excavating beneath an existing period house contributing to the delay. What began as an ambitious home improvement plan has evolved into a multimillion-pound construction project that is now approaching its third year of on-site work.From Victorian residence to luxury retreatAccording to The Standard, Dua purchased the three-storey Victorian Arts and Crafts property at the beginning of 2020 for £6.75 million. The singer, who grew up in the Hampstead area, had offered glimpses of the house during the Covid-19 lockdown, sharing photographs of its contemporary kitchen and striking marble bathroom on social media.However, the existing interiors were seemingly not the final vision for the property. In 2021, plans were submitted for a substantial transformation, with architect 4M Group appointed to oversee the proposed changes.The centrepiece of the redevelopment is a vast basement extension designed to accommodate a swimming pool, steam room, shower facilities, changing area and relaxation space. The underground level will also feature a private cinema and dedicated music studio, allowing Dua to work on creative projects without disturbing the residential spaces, The Standard report explains.The plans include separate studio workspaces, while the existing rear extension is being replaced with a redesigned family room featuring a green roof. The wider residential layout will retain three bedrooms, alongside a library, drawing room and an expansive open-plan kitchen and dining area.Why the renovation has taken so longAcording to reports, the project has faced considerable delays since its initial planning stages. The Daily Mail reported that conservationists and local planners opposed the singer's plans due to the property's location in a conservation area.The Redington Frognal Neighborhood Forum opposed the development because it would harm trees, boundary walls, and the environment. Neighborhood flooding and drain damage.Basement construction has caused subsidence, water management, and disturbance in Camden. After receiving planning approval, builders followed neighborhood safety rules.The Mirror UK reported that the planning process took three years, starting with applications in 2021 and construction in 2024.A massive underground construction operationThe scale of the excavation helps explain why the project has become such a lengthy undertaking. According to The Mirror UK, approximately 20 builders are currently involved in the work, which will expand the property's basement to around 310 square metres. The construction has already involved the removal of approximately 500 tonnes of soil, with excavation extending at least six metres underground.One of the biggest challenges has been protecting the 17 historic trees surrounding the property. Rather than undertaking conventional large-scale excavation, the construction team has had to adopt more careful methods to minimise vibration and protect the neighbouring structures, the online report adds.The Daily Mail previously reported that the approved construction arrangements included restrictions on noise and requirements for equipment to be mounted on anti-vibration isolators. The measures are crucial because nearby residents worry about the effects of extensive underground construction.Neighbors and conservation remain importantBeyond the architectural ambitions, the renovation has also involved balancing the singer's plans with the character of the surrounding neighbourhood. Environmental concerns raised during the planning process included the potential loss of green space, the removal of trees and possible disruption to natural drainage systems.The Mirror UK reports that measures have been introduced to limit the impact of construction, including controls covering noise, dust and waste management. Contact information has also been displayed at the site so residents and local businesses can raise concerns. The construction team has indicated its intention to minimise disruption throughout the redevelopment.Move-in date pushed to 2027Despite the lengthy planning process and extensive work already completed, Dua's London home is not expected to be ready until July 2027. The Mirror UK reports that the singer and her husband, actor Callum Turner, will therefore have to wait several more months before moving into the property. This massive investment will transform a historic London home into a modern home with dedicated spaces for relaxation, entertainment, and creative work.For now, the Victorian property remains a construction site rather than the finished family home Dua envisioned. With its underground leisure facilities, private cinema and music studio, the ambitious transformation is certainly far removed from an ordinary renovation.Images Courtesy: istock and InstagramYou use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, a Virginia couple in their 20s bought a $595,000 four-bedroom dream home without inspection; now they're ready to give up their 2.7% mortgage to escape it
articles.summary: A Virginia couple who bought what they thought was their perfect home in their 20s are now considering selling it, despite having locked in a mortgage
articles.body: A Virginia couple who bought what they thought was their perfect home in their 20s are now considering selling it, despite having locked in a mortgage rate of just 2.7%. Chloe, 32, and her husband Jake, 30, purchased the four-bedroom property in late 2020, but what initially seemed like a dream investment has gradually turned into a source of financial and personal stress.The couple recently opened up about their homeownership experience on the November 3 episode of personal finance author Ramit Sethi's podcast, I Will Teach You to Be Rich. Their story highlights how owning a house can bring unexpected responsibilities and expenses, even when buyers secure an unusually low mortgage rate.The couple purchased the property from Jake's parents in late 2020, taking it in its existing condition without getting a home inspection. The four-bedroom Virginia house has an office, a swimming pool and sits on 1.5 acres of land.According to Chloe, the property had once belonged to one of Jake's uncles, a multimillionaire whose grounds featured two koi ponds and a team of gardeners. However, much of the landscaping had been neglected by the time the couple took ownership.At the time, they were paying $2,400 a month in rent. Jake believed that mortgage rates were unlikely to fall much further and felt that renting was money going to waste. The house was appraised at $595,000, considerably higher than their original budget of $500,000.The mortgage was taken out in Jake's name alone. He explained that combining their credit scores would have put them below the 760 threshold they were aiming for, so Chloe was left off the loan.“Honestly, signing that though, like I wanted to throw up,” Jake recalled, referring to the roughly half-million-dollar loan.Their 2.7% mortgage comes with much higher ownership costsOne of the biggest reasons the couple has hesitated to sell is their exceptionally low mortgage rate. They locked in a 2.7% interest rate when the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate tracked by Freddie Mac was close to its record low of 2.65% in January 2021.The contrast with today's borrowing environment is significant. Freddie Mac's November 12 survey put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.11%. Data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency showed that only 19.2% of outstanding US mortgages had interest rates below 3% in the second quarter of 2026.The couple's monthly mortgage payment, including escrow, has increased from $2,990 to $3,072. However, once maintenance and other homeownership expenses are factored in, Chloe and Jake estimate that the property costs them closer to $4,500 a month.Yard work alone takes up approximately eight hours of their time on a typical weekend. For Chloe, who works as a software engineer, and Jake, a senior manager in an engineering department, maintaining the property has become an additional responsibility they no longer want.“Everybody that we talk to is like, you know, homeownership is the dream,” Chloe told Sethi. “And I'm like, are we just dumb?”An Airbnb plan, an expensive RV and other financial setbacksThe couple also admitted to making several financial decisions they now consider mistakes. Chloe referred to these ventures as their “schemes”.Around two years ago, they took out an $80,000 home equity loan to renovate the property with the intention of turning it into an Airbnb rental. However, they had barely researched the area's rental demand before committing to the plan. Chloe later acknowledged that demand for short-term rentals in the area was soft.They also purchased a 44-foot, eight-year-old recreational vehicle for $50,000, along with a new truck to tow it. However, getting the RV off their property proved so difficult that it never went on a trip. They eventually sold it two years later for between $30,000 and $32,000, taking a substantial loss.At the time of their appearance on Sethi's podcast, they still had approximately $45,000 outstanding on the home equity loan. They were putting around $7,000 a month towards clearing that debt, which they need to settle before selling the house.Ramit Sethi compares their financial future if they sell or stayDuring the podcast, Sethi examined the couple's finances and found that they were earning $30,166 a month before taxes, amounting to an annual household income of approximately $361,992.They also had $304,000 in investments, $68,000 in savings and a combined net worth of approximately $692,000.Jake has been in favour of selling the property and using the estimated $250,000 in home equity to invest in an S&P 500 index fund. His idea is to leave the money untouched and allow it to grow over the years, potentially securing a substantial part of their retirement savings while they are still young.Chloe, however, has found it difficult to make a final decision. She has agreed with Jake after discussing the numbers, only to begin questioning the decision again shortly afterwards. One of her concerns is that the property's value could continue to rise, making selling it now a missed opportunity.Sethi ran two possible retirement scenarios for the couple. If they kept the house and retired in 25 years, he estimated they could have approximately $4.8 million. If they sold the property and invested the equity, the figure could be closer to $6.2 million, although he noted that renting would likely eat into some of those gains.“One way or another, both of these decisions will be fine,” Sethi told them, steering the conversation away from simply comparing financial projections and towards what they actually wanted from their lives.The couple is reconsidering what homeownership means to themChloe had also considered renting out the property instead of selling it. However, she admitted that the yard had become a mess the last time they had tenants and that she would probably end up handling most of the responsibilities associated with managing renters.Sethi cautioned them against allowing the property to dictate their decisions. He pointed out that if they no longer owned the house, they would also no longer have to worry about maintaining its well and septic system.After months of going back and forth, Chloe appeared more open to the idea of moving on. She had previously spent around eight months debating whether selling the house would amount to another financial mistake.“We can buy another house if we want to,” she said towards the end of the conversation. “We have the money.”You use AI every day. articles.title: 'World’s most wanted girlfriend’ Vera Dijkmans detained by ICE, DHS reveals why she faces deportation
articles.summary: An OnlyFans model who once described herself as the “world's most wanted girlfriend” has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with her
articles.body: An OnlyFans model who once described herself as the “world's most wanted girlfriend” has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with her family raising concerns about the conditions in which she is being held at a New Jersey detention facility. Vera Dijkmans, 29, was reportedly handcuffed after arriving at Newark Liberty International Airport on a flight from Miami on November 11. She was taken to the Delaney Hall detention facility in New Jersey, according to her family.The Dutch influencer, who has nearly six million followers on Instagram and another 875,000 subscribers on OnlyFans, was travelling to New York to attend UFC 334 at Madison Square Garden, where she planned to create content with fighters.Why was Vera Dijkmans detained by ICE?According to her family, Dijkmans had missed an immigration court hearing after allegedly failing to receive a notification letter about the scheduled date. “There was a court date and she didn’t receive a letter so she missed her court case and didn’t know,” her sister, Iza Dijkmans, told the New York Post. “We consulted a lawyer, but since she has a removal order, they can’t do anything,” she added.Her mother, Marianne Scholt, told Dutch newspaper AD that her daughter had also missed an immigration appointment connected to her Green Card application. Scholt suggested that her daughter's frequent travel and hotel stays could have contributed to her missing the notification.“That is because she travels a lot. She also stays mostly in hotels and not at her permanent address. That is probably how she ended up in ICE’s systems,” she said.Dijkmans was reportedly in the US on a tourist visa, which does not permit visitors to work. Her mother acknowledged that her daughter had been creating content while in the country.Family alleges 'inhumane' conditions at ICE detention centreDijkmans' family has raised concerns about the conditions at the Delaney Hall detention facility, claiming that she is facing poor food, overcrowding and inadequate hygiene. Her sister said the influencer was sharing a room with 12 other detainees and was struggling with the conditions inside the facility.“Vera has shared deeply concerning details about the conditions she is facing,” Iza said.“She has told us that the food is very poor, the hygiene conditions are extremely unsanitary, and the atmosphere inside the facility is constantly tense.”She also alleged that Dijkmans felt intimidated by detention centre staff and was struggling to sleep because of an uncomfortable bed. “She hasn’t seen daylight for six days. The windows are sealed,” her sister claimed.Her mother travelled from the Netherlands to the US to visit her daughter and said she was distressed by what she saw.“Vera was in tears, and I barely recognized her in those prison clothes,” Scholt told AD.She claimed that Dijkmans' access to phone calls had been restricted, with her permitted calling time reduced from 45 minutes to five minutes. The facility reportedly has four phones available for approximately 60 detainees.The family has also contacted the Dutch Embassy in the US for assistance. A spokesperson for the Dutch government confirmed that officials were aware of the case and were providing consular assistance, but declined to disclose further details on privacy grounds.DHS reveals Vera Dijkmans' immigration historyAccording to DHS, US Customs and Border Protection arrested and removed her in March 2019 after she attempted to enter the country illegally through George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston.The department said she was then allowed to enter the US temporarily in August 2024 but overstayed her authorized stay. DHS also said she was placed in removal proceedings in August 2025 and that an immigration judge issued a final order of removal in May 2026 after she failed to appear for her hearing.A department spokesperson said a pending Green Card application does not automatically grant legal immigration status in the US.“She received due process and will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson said.Who is Vera Dijkmans?Dijkmans previously made headlines after claiming that around 5,000 men had applied to become her boyfriend. In 2023, the influencer invited men interested in dating her to submit applications detailing their jobs, living arrangements and previous relationships.She later spoke about her expectations from potential partners, saying that she wanted an impressive first date and a gift.“If they don’t suggest an impressive first date, I won’t bother going,” she told the Daily Mail in January 2025.“And he should bring you a gift, too.” She said she had received expensive clothing, including items from luxury brands Louis Vuitton and Hermès, but insisted that the gesture mattered more than the price.Despite receiving thousands of applications, the influencer reportedly did not find a romantic partner through the initiative.You use AI every day.
