articles.title: In 2018, a Michigan woman under guardianship signed a marital agreement providing her $705,000; she later argued an equal split should have brought nearly $1 million, but an appeals court upheld the deal in November 2026
articles.summary: A Michigan woman who signed a $705,000 marital property agreement while under legal guardianship has lost her appeal for a larger share of her former
articles.body: A Michigan woman who signed a $705,000 marital property agreement while under legal guardianship has lost her appeal for a larger share of her former husband's wealth. She argued that an equal division of their assets should have given her nearly $1 million. However, an appeals court has upheld the original agreement signed in 2018. The Michigan Court of Appeals issued its decision on 16 November 2026, rejecting Cassandra Fameux's challenge to the property settlement. The three-judge panel ruled that the original agreement was still legally binding. It also found that Fameux had not provided enough evidence to show that the agreement should be cancelled.The case involved her former husband, Paul Gregory St Claire, an anaesthesiologist who worked at the hospital where they first met. Fameux argued that the agreement was unfair because she was under a court-appointed guardianship when she signed it. She also questioned whether the legal protections required for someone in her situation had been properly followed. The appeals court rejected these arguments. It found that a lawyer had been appointed by the court to protect Fameux's interests during the earlier case. It also noted that the trial judge had reviewed the agreement and decided that the settlement was fair. According to the opinion published by Justia, the case is listed as Paul Gregory St Claire v Cassandra Fameux, docket number 378410. The appeal came from the Ingham Circuit Court, case number 23-002394-DM. Presiding Judge Michael J. Kelly wrote the court's per curiam opinion, which was also supported by Judges Michael J. Riordan and Michelle M. Rick.A marriage, children and legal guardianshipSt Claire and Fameux met in 2003 while working at the same hospital. He worked as an anaesthesiologist, while she was employed in the nutritional department. They married in 2009 after having two children together. During their marriage, Fameux was admitted to psychiatric hospitals several times. In 2015, her sister was appointed as her legal guardian. According to the Michigan Court of Appeals, Fameux testified that she remained close to her sister, including during the later divorce proceedings. In 2017, while Fameux was still under guardianship, St Claire filed a complaint for separate maintenance. This is a legal arrangement that allows married couples to live apart and settle their financial matters without ending their marriage. At the time, St Claire had obtained a personal protection order against Fameux. She violated the order before being admitted to hospital for a third time.St Claire told the court that Fameux had often said she wanted to divorce him. He said he chose to seek separate maintenance instead because it would allow her to remain on his health insurance. It would also help her qualify for his Social Security benefits after they had been married for another two years. He also raised concerns about the children's safety when they were in her care and what he described as her excessive spending. Fameux gave a different account of what happened. She testified that St Claire had told her the separate maintenance agreement was only meant to protect the family's finances. According to her, he assured her that it would not change their relationship and that they would continue living together as a family. After leaving hospital, she returned to the marital home. At the time, she was receiving long-acting antipsychotic injections for schizoaffective disorder. She claimed that her treatment was not appropriate and accused St Claire of deliberately giving her medication until she could no longer think clearly. St Claire denied the accusation.The $705,000 agreement signed in 2018During the separate maintenance case, both spouses had their own lawyers. Their legal teams agreed that Fameux needed additional protection. They arranged for attorney Melissa Leckie to represent Fameux's best interests under a September 2017 court order. The order gave Leckie the title of "Attorney-Guardian Ad Litem". The order instructed Leckie to protect Fameux's interests, review settlement offers and the proposed judgment with her, and attend court hearings when required. The couple reached an agreement through mediation. Under the Judgment of Separate Maintenance (JOSM), Fameux would receive $130,000 in cash. Another $575,000 would be transferred into her retirement account. Together, these payments were worth $705,000. St Claire also agreed to pay spousal support that could be adjusted over a period of five years.St Claire, Fameux, their lawyers and Leckie all signed the agreement. There was also a space for Fameux's sister to sign as her legal guardian. However, that signature line was crossed out after the lawyers agreed that her signature was not needed because Leckie had already been appointed to protect Fameux's interests. At a December 2017 hearing, the trial court decided that the division of assets was fair and approved the agreement. Fameux later testified that she did not understand what she had signed. She said neither her lawyer nor Leckie had properly explained the agreement to her. She also claimed that St Claire threatened that she would not be allowed to see their children unless she signed it. Court records show that the couple later started living together again. However, they gave different accounts of the relationship after they resumed living under the same roof.Woman argues she was pressured into signingWhen Fameux later challenged the agreement, she argued that she had been pressured into signing it while heavily medicated. She said she was unable to understand what the document meant or what she was agreeing to. She told the trial court that she would never have given up most of the couple's wealth if she had understood the agreement. She also blamed her legal representatives for failing to explain its terms properly. St Claire denied these claims. After hearing evidence from both sides, the trial judge rejected Fameux's allegation that St Claire and her legal representatives had worked together to take away her rights to marital property. The judge ruled that the agreement worked as a legally binding contract that settled how the couple's property would be divided. The court also rejected several requests to cancel the agreement.The trial court treated the division of property separately from future spousal support. The parties eventually agreed that Fameux could apply for additional support at a later date. The court also noted that St Claire had not followed every part of the agreement. However, Fameux had continued to benefit from using his credit cards. He had also made voluntary payments into her retirement account. The couple reached separate agreements on child custody and child support. These matters were settled without the court having to make a ruling.Appeals court rejects claim for a larger shareIn her appeal, Fameux argued that the 2018 agreement was unfair. She said an equal division of the couple's marital assets would have given her $995,368.50 instead of the $705,000 she received under the agreement. The Michigan Court of Appeals ruled that Fameux had not provided enough evidence to prove that the original division of assets was legally unfair. The judges noted that she had not shown any mistake in how the couple's assets were valued that would justify cancelling the agreement. The panel also considered the other benefits Fameux received under the deal. These included remaining on St Claire's health insurance and being able to qualify for his Social Security benefits after another two years of marriage. The judges referred to an earlier Michigan court decision, Berger v Berger. They explained that a fair division of marital property does not have to mean that both spouses receive exactly the same amount. A significant difference between the shares can still be fair if there is a good reason for it. Fameux also argued that the couple's decision to start living together again after signing the agreement should affect whether it remained valid.The appeals court disagreed. It referred to earlier decisions in Knapp v Knapp, Hagerty v Union Guardian Trust Co and Irvine v Irvine. These cases established that a couple getting back together does not automatically cancel every agreement they made while living apart. The judges explained that the 2018 agreement was designed to divide the couple's assets while allowing them to remain married and continue living together. It was not an agreement made in preparation for a divorce. For that reason, their decision to resume living together did not automatically cancel it. The panel also referred to the 2025 decision in Johnson v Johnson. That ruling confirmed that a consent judgment of separate maintenance is a legally binding contract unless there is evidence of fraud, mistake, illegality or unconscionability.Court upholds the original settlementThe appeals court also rejected Fameux's argument that the original case did not provide the proper legal protections required because she was under guardianship. She questioned why Leckie had been given the title of "Attorney-Guardian Ad Litem" instead of simply being appointed as a guardian ad litem. Fameux also pointed out that her sister, who was her legal guardian, had not signed the agreement. The judges ruled that Leckie's title did not change her main responsibilities. Her job was to protect Fameux's interests, take part in mediation and represent her in court. The panel also found that Leckie's failure to submit a separate written report did not make the agreement invalid. Her absence from the December 2017 court hearing did not invalidate it either. The judges noted that Leckie had signed the agreement.The court acknowledged that Fameux was under legal guardianship when she signed the agreement. It also did not assume that she personally understood every detail of the settlement. However, the judges pointed out that Fameux had not called Leckie, her former lawyer or her sister to give evidence in support of her claims. In its decision issued on 16 November 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's refusal to cancel the 2018 Judgment of Separate Maintenance. The panel also confirmed that the agreement could remain part of the couple's divorce judgment. As a result, the original $705,000 settlement remains legally binding, and Fameux will not receive the larger share of the marital assets she had requested.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bristol is putting floating gardens in its harbour as part of an £8.9 million plan for more than 200 wetland projects over five years to attract wildlife and reduce floods, aiming to become Britain’s first wetland city
articles.summary: Bristol is preparing to transform its urban landscape by bringing more nature into its waterways, streets and neighbourhoods through an ambitious wetland
articles.body: Bristol is preparing to transform its urban landscape by bringing more nature into its waterways, streets and neighbourhoods through an ambitious wetland restoration programme. The five-year initiative, led by the Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (WWT) with funding from insurer Aviva, will involve more than 200 projects designed to create habitats for wildlife, improve flood protection and make green spaces more accessible to residents. The development was reported by The Guardian, BBC News and Bristol24/7. With an investment of £8.9 million, the programme aims to help Bristol become the UK’s first accredited Wetland City under the Ramsar Convention, an international agreement dedicated to the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. The initiative will extend beyond the city’s harbour, bringing together a network of small and large wetland habitats. Plans include restoring river ecosystems, reconnecting rivers with their natural floodplains, developing rain gardens along streets and encouraging households to create small ponds that can support local biodiversity.Floating gardens bring wildlife back to the harbourOne of the first visible steps in the project began in September 2026, when floating wetlands were installed at three locations in Bristol’s city-centre harbour. These structures consist of buoyant platforms covered with wetland vegetation, creating small islands that provide shelter and feeding opportunities for birds, insects and other wildlife.The installations are designed to introduce natural habitats into an otherwise heavily developed urban environment. Early observations reportedly showed dragonflies and other wildlife arriving soon after the floating gardens were put in place. Ducks, swans and other waterbirds have also been seen using the new spaces.The project highlights how even relatively small interventions can help restore ecological connections in cities. Rather than treating urban waterways simply as transport routes or recreational spaces, the initiative aims to make them functioning ecosystems that support a wider range of species.How wetlands could help prevent floodingAlongside supporting wildlife, the programme is intended to address one of the growing challenges facing urban areas: managing excess rainwater during periods of heavy rainfall. Wetlands naturally absorb and store water, slowing its movement through the landscape. This can help reduce the volume of water entering drainage systems during storms, lowering pressure on infrastructure that can become overwhelmed during intense rainfall.Bristol’s project will therefore focus on managing rainwater closer to where it falls. Rain gardens, household ponds and restored waterways could all help capture runoff from roofs, roads and other built-up surfaces instead of allowing it to flow immediately into conventional drainage systems. The approach is particularly relevant as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather events in many parts of the UK. By restoring natural water-management systems, the city hopes to improve its resilience while creating more attractive public spaces.Why Bristol wants to become a wetland cityThe Wetland City Accreditation is part of the Ramsar Convention, which recognises urban areas that demonstrate a commitment to protecting and sustainably managing their wetland environments. There are already 74 accredited wetland cities across 27 countries, with China accounting for a significant share of them.Bristol was selected for the initiative partly because of its longstanding relationship with water. The city has approximately 100 miles of waterways, including several that are hidden beneath or incorporated into its urban infrastructure.The programme also aims to demonstrate that wetland restoration can deliver economic benefits alongside environmental improvements. Better waterfront spaces could attract more visitors, encourage businesses and increase activity in the city centre. The WWT hopes the investment will provide a model that other British towns and cities can eventually adopt.A wider vision for urban natureThe project comes at a time when cities are increasingly looking for ways to balance development with environmental protection. As urban populations grow, access to natural spaces and healthy ecosystems becomes increasingly important for both wildlife and residents.By connecting individual wetlands into larger wildlife corridors, Bristol hopes to create habitats that allow species to move through the city rather than remain isolated in small green spaces. The improvements could also give residents more opportunities to experience nature without having to travel to rural reserves. If successful, the programme could offer a practical example of how cities can use nature-based solutions to address flooding, biodiversity loss and the effects of a changing climate, while making everyday urban environments greener and more liveable.You use AI every day. articles.title: 2 held for Sidhrawali murder got Chinese gun from gangster, chatted on Signal
articles.summary: Two men arrested for the Sidhrawali murder allegedly got a Chinese Norinco PX-30 via gangster Lipin Nehra, coordinated on Signal, police say.
articles.body: Gurgaon: A probe into the murder of an alleged gangster near Sidhrawali bus stand on Nov 9 has revealed that two shooters arrested in the case were supplied weapons by fugitive gangster Lipin Nehra. The accused allegedly contacted Nehra’s associates through the encrypted messaging app, Signal, and were asked to collect the firearms from a pre-decided location in Palwal.Jatin (21) and Monu (27) – the two arrested accused – never met the person who had stashed the guns there, police said, pointing to how gangs are keeping arms suppliers and shooters apart to evade detection. According to cops, Monu had known a relative of Nehra for around 10 years. The accused first contacted the relative before reaching out to Nehra and his associates through Signal.“They found the weapons at the location shared with them on Signal. However, they did not know who had kept the firearms there. This is the modus operandi adopted by gangs, where the person supplying the weapons does not come face to face with the person collecting them,” a police officer said.Police recovered a country-made pistol, a foreign-made PX-30, seven live cartridges and a mobile phone from the accused. The PX-30 is the .30-bore variant of China’s Norinco PX-3 pistol. “It is an original PX-30, not a copy. The trail is suspected to be cross-border,” the officer said. Police suspect the gun was smuggled from Pakistan through Punjab.The accused allegedly did not pay for the firearms either. “Gang weapons are returned after the task is completed. Gangs also draw youngsters into their fold by helping them settle personal scores,” the officer said.Deepak (35), a Sidhrawali resident allegedly associated with the Ashok Rathi gang, was found dead in his Maruti Swift on Nov 9, his seat belt still fastened. CCTV footage showed a man approaching the car and opening fire. Police recovered 18 empty cartridges. Deepak had eight criminal FIRs registered against him in Gurgaon and Rajasthan, including two for murder, attempted murder, extortion and illegal arms possession.Police said the murder was the fallout of personal grudges, not a direct rivalry between Nehra and Deepak. Jatin allegedly wanted revenge for the assault on his brother and a friend by Deepak and his associates around six months ago. Monu, who had worked at a restaurant owned by Satyendra Yadav, allegedly held a grudge because Deepak had attempted to kill Yadav around six years ago. The two had been planning the murder for about 45 days, police said.Jatin allegedly brought Monu into the plan. articles.title: Scientists found only 22 wild northern copperbelly water snakes across Indiana, Michigan and Ohio in six years; 17 captive-bred juveniles have been released as efforts continue to save the threatened reptile
articles.summary: Scientists have documented just 22 wild northern copperbelly water snakes during six years of surveys across their northern range, highlighting the
articles.body: Scientists have documented just 22 wild northern copperbelly water snakes during six years of surveys across their northern range, highlighting the fragile state of one of the Midwest’s rarest reptiles. The US Fish and Wildlife Service conducted springtime surveys from 2020 through 2026, finding the snakes in only a few small, isolated locations across northern Indiana, southern Michigan and northwestern Ohio. To help rebuild the Great Lakes population, the agency partnered with the Toledo Zoo on a captive breeding programme. So far, 17 captive-bred juveniles have been released into suitable habitat, while another 10 are expected to be ready for release in 2027.Six years of surveys found only 22 wild northern copperbelly water snakesThe northern copperbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta) was listed as threatened in 1997 after populations declined sharply during the mid and late 1900s. The US Fish and Wildlife Service said its northern population represents the species at the northern extent of its range.From 2020 through 2026, biologists carried out springtime field surveys across the species’ northern range. Despite sustained efforts in the most well-studied population strongholds, they documented only 22 wild individuals. The agency stressed that the figure reflects the limits of survey coverage rather than a complete census of the species. Habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation have left the snakes in a few small, isolated locations, according to the US Fish and Wildlife Service.Captive breeding has produced 17 young snakes for release into the wildThe recovery effort began in 2020 with a captive breeding partnership between the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Toledo Zoo. Nineteen of the 22 documented snakes were brought into the programme, where they were health-checked, tested for snake fungal disease and incorporated into the breeding population. Two adult females have since successfully produced live young, while several other females may be pregnant.The programme has also improved survival among newborns, with about 71% surviving in captivity. As healthy juveniles reach their second summer, they are fitted with radio transmitters and released into suitable habitat near where their parents were captured. So far, 17 juveniles have been released, while another 10 are expected to be ready in 2027, the US Fish and Wildlife Service reported.Captive breeding alone cannot restore the population because the snakes depend on shallow wetlands connected by mature forests. They feed primarily on frogs, toads and tadpoles and may travel hundreds of metres between habitats. Since 2018, 17 habitat restoration projects have also been completed in Michigan, while 16.4 acres of forest and wetland habitat supporting the species were restored at Ohio’s Lake La Su An Wildlife Area in 2025, according to the agency.You use AI every day. articles.title: Houston police officer crashes into woman's car, leaving her with a broken leg; city denies compensation claim, then auctions the car for just $10; woman says she has lost her independence
articles.summary: A Houston woman who relied on her car as both a home and a place to keep her most treasured possessions says she was left without compensation after a
articles.body: A Houston woman who relied on her car as both a home and a place to keep her most treasured possessions says she was left without compensation after a police officer crashed into her vehicle. The situation became even more distressing when the damaged car was later declared abandoned and sold at an auction for just $10, without her knowledge, according to an investigation by ABC13 Houston.Kimberly Ezike said her vehicle was her lifeline when she was between places. It also contained some of her most valuable belongings, including the ashes of her late mother. But an accident on August 26, 2024, changed her circumstances, leaving her with a broken leg, no vehicle and an ongoing dispute with the city over compensation.Police officer's car crash left Kimberly Ezike injuredThe accident happened on Harwin Drive near Gessner Road in Houston. According to the Texas Department of Transportation crash report cited by ABC13 Houston, a Houston Police Department (HPD) officer responding to a burglary call struck Ezike's vehicle from behind.The impact pushed her car over the curb and into an electrical pole. Ezike suffered multiple injuries, including a broken leg.“He hit me really hard at a really high rate of speed,” she recalled while speaking to ABC13 Houston.Following the collision, her vehicle was towed to a storage facility that had a contract with HPD. Ezike said an officer at the scene told her that the car was being taken there for investigative purposes.City rejects compensation claim despite officer being suspendedAfter the accident, Ezike approached the city's legal department seeking compensation for her medical expenses and the damage to her car. However, her claim was rejected.The decision came despite internal HPD disciplinary records reportedly showing that the officer involved had been suspended for one day for failing to use caution in connection with the crash.Ezike questioned why the city would not accept responsibility for the accident.“If I hit one of them, especially from behind, I clearly would be responsible. So, they're telling me they're not responsible due to whatever, you know, they're the government or whatever else,” she told ABC13 Houston.She said she found the city's explanation difficult to accept, particularly because the department's own records documented disciplinary action against the officer.Car declared abandoned and sold at auction for $10The dispute took a more troubling turn when Ezike discovered that her vehicle had been classified as abandoned at the storage facility and sold through an HPD vehicle auction for just $10.The sale happened less than two months after the crash, in accordance with the department's policy for auctioning vehicles considered abandoned.Ezike, however, strongly disputes that description. She said she was waiting for the city to give her permission to pay the storage charges and retrieve her car. She also claimed that a city adjuster had told her the vehicle was still being used for an investigation.HPD told ABC13 Houston that Ezike had been notified that her vehicle was being considered abandoned and had been given a deadline to collect it.Records reviewed by the investigative team reportedly described the car as repairable. Ezike said she had never intended to abandon it, especially because several personal belongings were still inside.“That's all they thought my car was worth ... $10,” she said, reacting to the sale price.Among the belongings she says she lost were clothing, household items and her late mother's ashes.Why Houston denied her claim under governmental immunityWhen ABC13 Houston contacted the city for an explanation, its legal department said Ezike's claim had initially been denied under governmental immunity because the officer was responding to an emergency call.Under the Texas Tort Claims Act, governmental immunity can be waived in certain cases involving motor vehicle accidents caused by government employees acting within the scope of their duties. However, Section 101.055 provides protection for government employees responding to emergencies, subject to exceptions involving conscious indifference or reckless disregard for the safety of others.In Ezike's case, the city reportedly relied on the officer's emergency response as the basis for rejecting her claim.The crash report also included Ezike's account of what happened before the collision. She reportedly told officials that she saw the officer's emergency lights and initially thought she was being pulled over. She slowed down and attempted to move into a parking lot to make way for the officer, but he struck her car.Houston reviewing thousands of claims against police departmentEzike's experience has come under renewed attention as Houston reviews compensation claims involving its police department.The issue gained prominence after a University of Houston student's car was damaged by police gunfire in Highland Village during an incident in which officers opened fire on a suspect. Following media attention, the city revisited the student's case and provided her with a replacement vehicle.Mayor John Whitmire subsequently announced a review of previously filed claims, acknowledging that the city had apparently followed a general practice of declaring governmental immunity in such cases.ABC13 Houston's investigation found that the city had paid approximately one in every four personal injury or property damage claims filed against HPD since 2024. The investigation also found that records from the city's legal department did not provide an explanation for why individual claims had been denied.The city later informed the news outlet that its legal department was reviewing approximately 2,000 claims dating back to July 2023. Officials did not disclose how many had been examined by the time of the report and said no previously denied claims had been reversed.Woman says she has lost her independence after the accidentFor Ezike, the consequences of the crash have extended far beyond the loss of her vehicle. In the nearly two years since the incident, she says she has had to depend on public transport, Lyft and hired taxi drivers to travel around Houston.She believes her case deserves the same consideration as the University of Houston student's claim, particularly because the accident affected her ability to move around and maintain her livelihood.When asked whether her case should be included in the city's review, she said it should absolutely be reconsidered.“They tore up my car, they stopped my livelihood. Yes, of course, mine is just as important as hers,” she told ABC13 Houston.Ezike is still waiting for the city to reconsider her claim. Meanwhile, the review of thousands of cases has raised questions about how Houston evaluates complaints involving police vehicles and why some residents are denied compensation even when internal disciplinary records document an officer's failure to exercise caution.You use AI every day. articles.title: George and Amal Clooney founded a justice organisation that challenges unfair trials and defends human rights; its legal programmes support journalists, women and girls across more than 40 countries
articles.summary: The work of a legal rights organisation rarely follows the pace of a news cycle.
articles.body: The work of a legal rights organisation rarely follows the pace of a news cycle. Cases can remain unresolved for years, laws may take even longer to change, and people facing discrimination or imprisonment often struggle to find legal representation. It was against this backdrop that George and Amal Clooney established the Clooney Foundation for Justice, an organisation focused on providing legal support to people whose rights have been violated. Working across more than 40 countries, the foundation concentrates on two broad areas: defending freedom of speech and advancing the rights of women and girls. Its work includes representing journalists, supporting survivors of violence and challenging legal systems that deny people a fair hearing.How the Clooney Foundation for Justice began its workThe Clooney Foundation for Justice (CFJ) was established by actor George Clooney and human rights lawyer Amal Clooney to address inequalities in access to justice. Rather than concentrating on a single country or category of legal disputes, the organisation works internationally, offering free legal assistance to people who might otherwise struggle to challenge unfair treatment through the courts.Its activities extend beyond individual cases. The foundation monitors criminal proceedings, reports on trials where fairness is in question and takes legal action against laws it considers unjust. It also helps establish legal aid clinics for vulnerable communities and supports younger advocates working in the field of gender justice.Reportedly, the organisation's work is spread across more than 40 countries, reflecting the range of legal and human rights issues it addresses. Some cases require immediate intervention, while others involve years of legal proceedings before any meaningful progress becomes visible.Two programmes focus on journalists and women's rightsThe foundation operates through two principal initiatives, each addressing a different area of legal vulnerability. TrialWatch concentrates on freedom of speech and the treatment of journalists facing criminal prosecution or imprisonment. Waging Justice for Women, meanwhile, provides legal assistance to women and girls dealing with discrimination, violence and restrictions on their rights.Together, the programmes form the main part of CFJ's legal aid work. Both involve supporting individuals through legal processes while documenting wider problems within the justice systems in which their cases arise.TrialWatch works to defend journalists facing unfair imprisonmentThrough its TrialWatch initiative, the foundation provides free legal representation to journalists who have been imprisoned in circumstances where their right to a fair trial is in question. The programme also monitors criminal proceedings internationally, making it possible to identify cases where legal protections may not have been properly observed.The initiative is designed to address more than the circumstances of individual journalists. By examining how criminal trials are conducted, TrialWatch also seeks to bring attention to broader concerns surrounding press freedom and the use of legal systems against people reporting on matters of public interest.CFJ describes the programme as the first initiative of its kind to monitor criminal trials globally. Its approach combines legal assistance with the documentation of proceedings, giving the organisation a basis for raising concerns about cases in which journalists face imprisonment.Waging Justice for Women provides legal support to women and girlsThe foundation's second programme, Waging Justice for Women, focuses on people whose rights are affected by discrimination, child marriage and violence. It provides free legal assistance to women and girls, including those seeking protection from practices that restrict their freedom or prevent them from exercising their legal rights.The programme recognises that access to legal representation can be particularly difficult for women facing abuse or discrimination. Without appropriate support, challenging such treatment through the courts can become difficult, especially in communities where established social practices and legal barriers overlap.Through this initiative, CFJ works to help women and girls pursue legal remedies and defend their rights. The programme also contributes to the foundation's wider efforts to support gender justice advocates and improve access to legal assistance.Supporting survivors of atrocities beyond the headlinesSome of the foundation's work concerns human rights violations that continue to affect survivors long after international attention has moved elsewhere. CFJ says it remains involved in cases involving atrocities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sudan, alongside efforts to address violence and discrimination against women and girls in different parts of the world.One of the causes closely associated with Amal Clooney's legal work is the pursuit of justice for Yazidi women who were raped and enslaved by Islamic State (ISIS). The foundation identifies her representation of these women as part of its continuing efforts to secure accountability for crimes committed against vulnerable communities.Such cases can involve complicated legal proceedings and lengthy efforts to establish responsibility. The passage of time does not necessarily bring an end to the legal difficulties faced by survivors, particularly when those responsible for abuses have not been brought before a court.CFJ's stated approach is to continue working on these matters even when they no longer receive sustained media coverage. Its work combines individual legal representation with wider efforts to challenge discriminatory laws and improve the availability of legal support.Why the foundation's work can take yearsLegal action in cases involving human rights violations does not always produce quick results. Investigations, court proceedings and efforts to challenge existing legislation can stretch across several years. In some situations, survivors must also contend with legal systems that offer limited protection or make it difficult to hold perpetrators accountable.The foundation acknowledges that the route to justice can be lengthy, particularly in cases involving violence, discrimination and restrictions on freedom of expression. Its programmes are therefore structured around continued legal assistance rather than short-term interventions.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Goldy Dhillon a petty thief': Lawrence gang on gangster who threatened Amitabh Bachchan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Gangster Goldy Dhillon had a narrow escape in Germany during an attack by the Lawrence Bishnoi gang's Canada handler, Manna Brampton, and his
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Gangster Goldy Dhillon had a narrow escape in Germany during an attack by the Lawrence Bishnoi gang's Canada handler, Manna Brampton, and his Madrid counterpart, Mandeep Spain, in Jan this year, the duo said in a statement on social media Tuesday.A day after Dhillon's post threatening actor Amitabh Bachchan, the duo hit out at Dhillon for killing an LGBTQ+ influencer, Mad Sandhu, in Amritsar and called him "publicity hungry" for targeting Bachchan.Claiming Dhillon used to wash utensils at a restaurant in Germany for a living, they said he lacked the wherewithal to target Bachchan or even his domestic staff.Calling Dhillon's claims of seeking revenge for the 1984 anti-Sikh riots a desperate bid for attention, Brampton and Spain said he was no-thing more than a petty thief and a "chitta" (heroin) peddler from Punjab with FIRs against him for drug-dealing and stealing cable wires.On the attack, the gang said despite constantly boasting about weapons, Dhillon had nothing but a knife to defend himself. He managed to escape and subsequently fled the country, they claimed.Furthermore, the former associates said they were the ones who had helped Dhillon gain a footing in the underworld by carrying out for free three murders and 20-25 firings in Canada to establish his name.In a damning blow to his credibility in the underworld, Brampton and Spain also labelled Dhillon a police informer. They claimed after using henchmen to commit crimes, Dhillon would tip off cops to get his operatives arrested, while posting about the incidents online to take credit. Challenging Dhillon to a face-off in any country, the duo warned others against associating with him.The post, sources said, prima facie confirmed speculation that Dhillon had parted ways with the Lawrence gang. In his post against Bachchan Monday, Dhillon did not mention Lawrence Bishnoi, even as he named a number of operatives, including Rocky Portugal and Suman Germany.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Alabama man won a $126,504.64 judgment after stormwater from a neighbouring subdivision damaged his land, but struggled to collect it; in November 2026, the state's highest court dismissed his latest appeal
articles.summary: A property owner in Alabama secured a six-figure court judgment after stormwater runoff from a neighbouring residential subdivision repeatedly damaged his
articles.body: A property owner in Alabama secured a six-figure court judgment after stormwater runoff from a neighbouring residential subdivision repeatedly damaged his land. However, winning the case did not mean he could easily recover the money. After encountering difficulties collecting the award and alleging that the homeowners' association had taken steps to avoid paying it, he launched another legal battle involving the association, its board members and residents of the subdivision.The Supreme Court of Alabama, in its November 13, 2026, decision in Carpenter v. Jacobs, available on Justia, dismissed his latest appeal without examining the underlying claims. The court's decision centred on a procedural issue: whether the lower court had properly allowed an appeal to proceed before the remaining claims in the wider dispute had been resolved.Stormwater damage led to a $200,000 jury awardThe dispute dates back to 2018, when William D. Carpenter alleged that rainwater flowing from a drainage easement in the Crown Pointe residential subdivision in Mobile County, Alabama, was damaging his property. He claimed that the runoff travelled downhill from the area behind four neighbouring lots and repeatedly affected his land.In July 2020, Carpenter filed a lawsuit against the Crown Pointe Owners' Association (CPOA) and four homeowners whose properties were closest to his. He accused them of negligence, trespass, nuisance, wantonness and negligent channelisation of water. Before the case went to trial, he reached settlement agreements with three of the homeowners, Janine Wallace, Betty Smith Lott and Myrtle F. Smith.In April 2022, a jury awarded Carpenter $200,000 against the homeowners' association. However, the court deducted $84,000 received through the settlements, leaving him with a judgment of $126,504.64, including costs. Despite the favourable verdict, collecting the remaining amount proved difficult.Homeowners' association faced allegations of avoiding paymentAccording to the court record, Carpenter managed to garnish just $1,516.18 from the association's bank account in August 2022. He subsequently alleged that the association's board had opened another checking account in the names of two board members, Barbara Cain and Mary Roberts, and instructed residents to pay their dues and assessments to them instead of the association.The CPOA filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2023. Meanwhile, its board voted to establish another organisation, the Crown Pointe West Homeowners' Association (CPWHA), in August 2023. Residents were subsequently instructed to make their payments to the newly formed association. The bankruptcy court dismissed the CPOA's bankruptcy petition in July 2024.Carpenter also alleged that the original association had arranged drainage work behind the four properties in an attempt to address the continuing water problem. The work was reportedly carried out in March 2023 after a contractor submitted a proposal for drainage improvements. The association had also levied a special assessment on the subdivision's 21 lots to cover the expense.In August 2024, Carpenter filed another lawsuit against both homeowners' associations, their board members and the subdivision's lot owners. He sought to hold additional parties responsible for the continuing drainage damage and the unpaid 2022 judgment.Why the Alabama Supreme Court dismissed the appealThe second lawsuit involved several claims, including negligence, nuisance, trespass and allegations that the defendants had taken steps to prevent Carpenter from collecting his earlier judgment. He also argued that the individual lot owners had an undivided interest in the subdivision's common property, including the drainage easement, making them potentially responsible for its maintenance. However, several homeowners challenged the claims, arguing that they did not own the drainage easement and had not personally contributed to the alleged water damage. Wallace and Smith also relied on their earlier settlement agreements, which contained provisions restricting future water-related claims against them.In February 2025, the Mobile Circuit Court enforced the settlement releases involving Wallace and Smith, dismissing Carpenter's claims against them. In February 2026, it separately dismissed his claims against the non-board-member lot owners. On February 23, 2026, the court issued an amended order certifying the dismissals as final under Rule 54(b), allowing Carpenter to appeal before the entire case was concluded.The Supreme Court of Alabama examined whether this certification was legally appropriate. Under Rule 54(b), a court can allow an appeal involving some parties or claims to proceed before the remaining matters are resolved, but only when there is no just reason for delaying the appeal. The justices found that the dismissed claims were closely connected to those still pending in the lower court. The outcome of the remaining proceedings could determine whether the individual homeowners had any responsibility for the drainage problems or the unpaid judgment. It could also make an appeal concerning their dismissal unnecessary.On November 13, 2026, the Supreme Court therefore dismissed Carpenter's appeal because the lower court had improperly certified its orders as final. Importantly, the justices did not rule on whether the dismissed homeowners were liable, whether the settlement releases prevented further claims or whether the association had attempted to avoid paying the judgment. The underlying dispute against the association and its remaining board members was still pending. The latest ruling was therefore a procedural dismissal, not a decision overturning Carpenter's original $126,504.64 judgment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
